5.notes: Hint 3 fails the standard's own test: 'if a student can answer by reading hint 3 alone, without thinking, it is too strong.' The exact words are: 'the other is linked with the front edge of a traditional stage. Use the curtain and the audience as your landmarks: which position does the stem describe?' This simply hands back the question's own wording ('the part of the theatre in front of the curtain'). Centre stage is self-evidently 'the middle' from its own name, so by elimination the student lands on proscenium purely by phrase-matching, with no engagement with what a proscenium actually is. Compare to the other hint 3s in this batch (e.g. Q17, Q20, Q30, Q31), which all require a real inferential step (classifying a word, judging a connotation, applying an outside fact) rather than restating the stem.
5.fix: Of the two stage terms left, one names a fixed point in the middle of the acting area, one that would still exist even if there were no curtain at all. The other only makes sense because of the curtain and the arch that frames a traditional stage. If the curtain were taken away, which of the two terms would lose its meaning, and is that the position the stem is asking about?

33.notes: Hint 3 says: "Three of the options are ways of naming the wood." A student can answer from this clause alone, without any knowledge of the play, simply by scanning the four options and noting that A, C and D all contain the word 'wood' while B does not: B is then the only option left, which is the settled answer. This collapses the choice to one option by counting words in the option text rather than by testing the student's grasp of the play's sequence of scenes, so hint 3 makes the choice for the student instead of narrowing to a genuine final decision.
33.fix: This speech is spoken while Egeus's complaint is still being heard at court, before Lysander and Hermia have made any plan to escape. Ask yourself whether the scene is happening in the city, in front of the Duke, or already out in the wood, and choose from there.
